one_liner: Portable C89 YAML 1.1 parser/emitter (the engine under PyYAML's C loaders); about 6-7x yaml-cpp's YAML::Load throughput.
what_it_does: LibYAML is a small C library for parsing and emitting YAML. It has three layers: a token scanner (yaml_parser_scan), an event parser (yaml_parser_parse, one event per call), and a document loader (yaml_parser_load) that builds an index-based yaml_document_t of string scalars, sequences and mappings. The emitter mirrors this with an event API and a document dumper. It is not a drop-in for yaml-cpp: there is no typed Node, no operator[] lookup and no as<T>() conversion, so you consume events or walk the document yourself.
how_it_is_fast: It is a hand-written two-stage pipeline: a scanner with a token queue, a 'simple key' lookahead and an indentation stack for block collections, feeding an LL(1) recursive-descent parser written as an explicit state machine that emits events one at a time. Input passes through a 16 KB raw buffer that is decoded and validated into a 48 KB UTF-8 buffer, and nothing is materialised unless you call the loader. So the cost is one pass, a character-by-character copy of each scalar into a growable string and one malloc per scalar, anchor or tag. There is no SIMD and no zero-copy path. That copying is why in-place parsers such as rapidyaml are 3-4x faster than libyaml on the same file, while libyaml still beats yaml-cpp's DOM-building YAML::Load by about 6-7x.
when_to_use: C or C++ code that needs a YAML parser and emitter every Linux distribution already packages, with a stable C ABI (libtool-versioned shared library) and no dependencies beyond libc.
Hot config-loading paths currently using yaml-cpp's YAML::Load, where you can consume events or build your own light tree: 86.79 vs 11.71 MB/s on a 4 KB CI file in rapidyaml's suite.
Streaming large or multi-document input through the event API (yaml_parser_parse) without building a tree; memory stays at the fixed reader buffers plus the current event.
When parse results must match PyYAML's C loaders or other language bindings that wrap libyaml.
Generating YAML from C with the event-level emitter or yaml_emitter_dump.
when_not_to_use: Peak parse throughput: rapidyaml's ryml_yaml_* rows parse the same travis.yml at 286.67-346.22 MB/s against libyaml's 86.79 MB/s (3.3-4.0x, derived from page data), and catalogued siblings yam and yeptris claim 1.6-13x and 2.2-4.1x over libyaml.
You want a typed, queryable DOM (node["key"].as<int>()): libyaml returns string scalars with style and tag only and does no type resolution.

Strict YAML 1.2 behaviour: the scanner follows the 1.1 grammar (since 0.2.3 it accepts %YAML 1.2 directives); open issue #351 (GLD Serializer Benchmark) reports spec-compliance misses in 0.2.5; libfyaml targets 1.2.

Untrusted, deeply nested input on the 0.2.5 release that distributions ship: nesting limits exist only on master and in 0.2.6-rc.1, and issue #251 (the loader cycles on 1,048,576 '{' characters) is still open.
You need a custom allocator or arena: yaml_malloc/yaml_realloc/yaml_free call malloc/realloc/free directly (feature request #178 open since 2020).

integration.form: static lib or shared lib (autotools or CMake build; packaged as libyaml in most distributions)
integration.min_toolchain: C89 compiler; CMake 3.10+ on current master, or autoconf/libtool/make (./bootstrap) for a git checkout
integration.platforms: any: portable C with no SIMD or architecture-specific code; Linux, macOS and Windows (CMake/MSVC, YAML_DECLARE_STATIC for static builds)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Parser and emitter state lives in per-object structs, so use one yaml_parser_t per thread; the exception is the master-only nesting limit, a process-wide plain int (MAX_NESTING_LEVEL, default 1000) changed by yaml_set_max_nest_level without synchronisation.

gotchas: Harness flaw (output fidelity, not speed): rapidyaml's LibyamlParser wrapper (bm/libyaml.hpp) discards libyaml's decoded scalar and stores the raw source slice m_input.str + start_mark.index instead. libyaml's mark.index counts characters, not bytes (SKIP/READ do index++ while advancing the pointer by the UTF-8 width), so on any non-ASCII input the slices are shifted. Quoted, escaped and block scalars are stored undecoded, and aliases are a no-op case. travis.yml is pure ASCII (4067 bytes, no anchors), and the timed loop still includes libyaml's full scan plus its per-scalar malloc'd copies, so the headline row is not inflated. It does measure libyaml events plus a cheap borrowed-string ryml tree, not libyaml's own yaml_parser_load DOM, for which no number exists.

Unequal versions and a single run: libyaml is cloned from master at build time (post-0.2.5 nesting-limit commits), while yaml-cpp is pinned to commit 587b24e2 of 2019-11-30, between 0.6.3 and 0.7.0, so it misses later yaml-cpp releases. Each row is one Google Benchmark repetition (14930 vs 2024 iterations), and the result JSON names the binary ryml-bm-parse-0.15.2.

A parser takes its input only once: yaml_parser_set_input_string/_file/set_input assert(!parser->read_handler), so you must call yaml_parser_delete and yaml_parser_initialize per document stream. Under NDEBUG the assert is compiled out and the misuse goes unchecked. Do not mix yaml_parser_load with yaml_parser_scan/yaml_parser_parse on one parser.

Security record: past fuzzing found heap overflows and stack overflows, mostly in the emitter, now closed. Issues for CVE-2024-35325/35326/35328/35329 are still open; the maintainer disputes 35326/35328/35329 as API misuse (structs not initialised with the library's init functions).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick libyaml over rapidyaml, fkYAML or libfyaml when you want a plain-C dependency that every distribution already ships and whose behaviour matches PyYAML and the other libyaml bindings. Pick rapidyaml (3.3-4.0x faster on the same file), yam or yeptris when throughput matters, and libfyaml when you need YAML 1.2 with a C document API.
verified_claims_summary: In rapidyaml's own parse suite (bm/bm_parse.cpp, Google Benchmark v1.9.5, g++ 16.1 Release C++17 per the build-directory name, 20 logical CPUs at 4279 MHz whose 1 MiB L2 and 19.25 MiB L3 fit a 10-core part, model not named, scaling and ASLR off, one repetition on 2026-07-07), libyaml master events fed into a ryml tree parsed the 4067-byte travis.yml at 86.79 MB/s (0.047 ms). yaml-cpp's YAML::Load (2019 commit 587b24e2) reached 11.71 MB/s (0.347 ms), 7.41x slower; the README's compile_commands.json row shows 135.06 vs 22.53 MB/s (6.00x).
status_note: Active but slow-moving: the last stable release is 0.2.5 (June 2020), 0.2.6-rc.1 was tagged in April 2026 and master last changed on 2026-08-21 (nest-depth getter); MIT-licensed, small portable C, so taking it from distribution packages or vendoring it is low-risk.
